drugs.name: Bethanechol

fields.action: Direct-acting muscarinic agonist that selectively binds to and activates muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, stimulating the parasympathetic nervous system. It increases tone in the bladder detrusor muscle to prompt urination and enhances gastrointestinal smooth muscle tone and peristalsis.
fields.dosage:
FORMS / STRENGTHS
Oral tablets: 5 mg, 10 mg, 25 mg, 50 mg. Subcutaneous injection: 5 mg/mL.
DOSE / SCOPE
Adult nonobstructive urinary retention: 10-50 mg orally 3-4 times daily; individualized to response.
fields.indication: Treatment of acute postoperative and postpartum nonobstructive (functional) urinary retention, and neurogenic atony of the urinary bladder with retention.
fields.contraindication: Hypersensitivity, mechanical gastrointestinal or urinary obstruction, hyperthyroidism, peptic ulcer disease, active or latent bronchial asthma, pronounced bradycardia, hypotension, and coronary artery disease.
fields.adverse: Severe drop in blood pressure with reflex tachycardia, syncope, bronchospasm, heart block, and cardiac arrest.
fields.effects: Abdominal discomfort, cramps, excessive salivation, diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, sweating, flushing, headache, and urinary urgency.
fields.notes: Should be taken on an empty stomach (1 hour before or 2 hours after meals) to minimize nausea and vomiting. Atropine sulfate is the specific antidote for overdosage.

drugs.name: Pilocarpine

fields.action: Direct-acting cholinergic parasympathomimetic agent that stimulates muscarinic receptors, causing contraction of the iris sphincter (miosis) and ciliary muscle, and stimulation of exocrine (salivary) glands.
fields.dosage:
FORMS / STRENGTHS
Ophthalmic solution: 0.5%, 1%, 2%, 3%, 4%, 6%. Ophthalmic gel: 4%. Oral tablets (saligen): 5 mg.
DOSE / SCOPE
Adult radiation-related dry mouth: start 5 mg orally 3 times daily. Sjogren syndrome: 5 mg orally 4 times daily.
fields.indication: Management of chronic open-angle glaucoma, acute angle-closure glaucoma, and treatment of symptoms of xerostomia (dry mouth) caused by salivary gland hypofunction or Sjögren’s syndrome.
fields.contraindication: Acute inflammation of the anterior chamber, hypersensitivity, secondary glaucoma where constriction is undesirable, and uncontrolled asthma or severe acute cardiac disease.
fields.adverse: Retinal detachment, paradoxical increase in intraocular pressure, and systemic cholinergic toxicity (hypotension, bronchospasm).
fields.effects: Blurred vision, decreased night vision, brow ache, eye irritation, lacrimation, increased sweating, flushing, and rhinitis.
fields.notes: Caution patients about driving or performing hazardous tasks at night due to impaired vision from miosis.

drugs.name: Muscarine

fields.action: A natural, potent direct-acting muscarinic receptor agonist that mimics acetylcholine at parasympathetic neuroeffector junctions, leading to excessive parasympathetic overstimulation.
fields.dosage:
FORMS / STRENGTHS
Not an FDA-approved pharmaceutical drug; available strictly as a research toxin or standard reference compound (isolated naturally from Amanita muscaria and other mushrooms).
DOSE / SCOPE
No therapeutic human dose. This is a toxin entry, not a medicine regimen.
fields.indication: None clinically approved (used primarily in pharmacological research to study muscarinic pathways).
fields.contraindication: N/A (Toxin; not used therapeutically).
fields.adverse: Severe cholinergic poisoning profile (SLUDGE: Salivation, Lacrimation, Urination, Defecation, Gastrointestinal distress, Emesis), severe miosis, extreme bradycardia, hypotension, and fatal bronchoconstriction.
fields.effects: Profuse sweating, excessive salivation, blurred vision, abdominal cramping, and severe vomiting.
fields.notes: Muscarine is not broken down by acetylcholinesterase, contributing to its high toxicity profile. Treated medically with atropine as an antidote.

drugs.name: Nicotine

fields.action: Binds to and stimulates nicotinic acetylcholine receptors in the central nervous system, adrenal medulla, autonomic ganglia, and neuromuscular junctions, prompting the release of dopamine and other neurotransmitters.
fields.dosage:
FORMS / STRENGTHS
Transdermal patches: 7 mg/24hr, 14 mg/24hr, 21 mg/24hr. Chewing gum/lozenges: 2 mg, 4 mg. Inhaler: 10 mg cartridge. Nasal spray: 10 mg/mL.
DOSE / SCOPE
Adult cessation: one patch daily. More than 10 cigarettes/day: example label starts 21 mg/day for 4 weeks, then 14 mg/day for 2 weeks, then 7 mg/day for 2 weeks. Lower intake starts at 14 mg.
fields.indication: Nicotine replacement therapy (NRT) for smoking cessation and relief of nicotine withdrawal symptoms.
fields.contraindication: Immediate post-myocardial infarction period, severe or worsening angina pectoris, severe cardiac arrhythmias, and active temporal/jaw TMJ disorders (for gum).
fields.adverse: Tachycardia, hypertension, cardiac arrhythmias, and acute nicotine toxicity (seizures, respiratory failure).
fields.effects: Local skin irritation (patch), mouth irritation or hiccups (gum/lozenge), insomnia, headache, dizziness, nausea, and vivid dreams.
fields.notes: Advise patients to completely stop smoking while using any nicotine replacement product to avoid dangerous cardiovascular spikes.

drugs.name: Varenicline

fields.action: Partial agonist-antagonist that binds selectively to alpha-4 beta-2 nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, reducing feelings of pleasure derived from nicotine while alleviating withdrawal symptoms.
fields.dosage:
FORMS / STRENGTHS
Oral tablets: 0.5 mg and 1 mg (often sold in continuation or starter packs).
DOSE / SCOPE
Adult smoking cessation: 0.5 mg daily on days 1-3, 0.5 mg twice daily on days 4-7, then 1 mg twice daily. Typical course: 12 weeks.

fields.contraindication: Hypersensitivity to varenicline or its excipients.

fields.effects: Nausea (most common), insomnia, abnormal/vivid dreams, constipation, flatulence, and dry mouth.
fields.notes: Should be taken with food and a full glass of water to help minimize treatment-related nausea.

drugs.name: Succinylcholine

fields.action: A depolarizing skeletal muscle relaxant. It mimics acetylcholine, binding to nicotinic receptors at the neuromuscular junction to cause prolonged depolarization, rendering the motor end-plate resistant to further activation by ACh.
fields.dosage:
FORMS / STRENGTHS
Solution for injection /IV infusion: 20 mg/mL, 50 mg/mL, 100 mg/mL.
DOSE / SCOPE
Adult short-procedure/intubation label: average 0.6 mg/kg IV; specialist anesthetic and airway management required.
fields.indication: Adjunct to general anesthesia to facilitate endotracheal intubation and to relax skeletal muscles during surgery or mechanical ventilation.
fields.contraindication: Personal or family history of malignant hyperthermia, major burns, massive skeletal muscle trauma, extensive denervation of skeletal muscle, and pre-existing hyperkalemia.
fields.adverse: Malignant hyperthermia, severe hyperkalemia (which can cause cardiac arrest), cardiac arrhythmias, and prolonged apnea.
fields.effects: Postoperative muscle fasciculations and transient muscle pain (myalgia).
fields.notes: Has a rapid onset (under 1 minute) and very short duration of action (5 to 10 minutes). Must be administered only by personnel skilled in airway management.

drugs.name: Edrophonium

fields.action: A short-acting reversible indirect-acting acetylcholinesterase inhibitor. It reversibly binds to the active center of acetylcholinesterase, temporarily preventing the breakdown of acetylcholine and amplifying cholinergic effects at both muscarinic and nicotinic receptor sites.
fields.dosage:
FORMS / STRENGTHS
Intravenous/Intramuscular injection: 10 mg/mL.
DOSE / SCOPE
Historical diagnostic protocols exist; a current routine-use dosing label was not confirmed in this review.
fields.indication: Differential diagnosis of myasthenia gravis (Tensilon test) and evaluation of acute myasthenic crises vs. cholinergic crises; also used as a temporary reversal agent for non-depolarizing neuromuscular blocking drugs.
fields.contraindication: Known hypersensitivity, mechanical intestinal or urinary obstruction.
fields.adverse: Severe bradycardia, laryngospasm, bronchoconstriction, and cardiac arrhythmias or arrest.
fields.effects: Increased salivation, lacrimation, diaphoresis, nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramps, and miosis.
fields.notes: Due to its ultra-short duration of action (about 5–10 minutes) and the risk of profound bradycardia, an antagonist like atropine sulfate must always be immediately available during administration.

drugs.name: Neostigmine

fields.action: Reversible indirect-acting acetylcholinesterase inhibitor that forms a covalent carbamyl-enzyme complex, inhibiting the breakdown of acetylcholine and increasing its availability at neuromuscular junctions and autonomic synapses.
fields.dosage:
FORMS / STRENGTHS
Solution for injection: 0.5 mg/mL, 1 mg/mL. Oral tablets: 15 mg.
DOSE / SCOPE
Adult reversal: 0.03-0.07 mg/kg IV; maximum 0.07 mg/kg or 5 mg, whichever is less. Give with atropine or glycopyrrolate.
fields.indication: Reversal of effects of non-depolarizing neuromuscular blocking agents after surgery; symptomatic management of myasthenia gravis.
fields.contraindication: Peritonitis, mechanical obstruction of the intestinal or urinary tract, and known hypersensitivity.
fields.adverse: Severe bronchospasm, cardiovascular depression, bradycardia, and cholinergic crisis.
fields.effects: Muscle twitching, excessive salivation, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal cramps, and urinary frequency.
fields.notes: Often administered alongside an anticholinergic agent (such as atropine or glycopyrrolate) to block unwanted muscarinic side effects like severe bradycardia.

drugs.name: Pyridostigmine

fields.action: Reversible acetylcholinesterase inhibitor that prolongs the action of acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction. It has a longer duration of action compared to neostigmine.
fields.dosage:

Adult myasthenia gravis: dose and intervals individually titrated. The reviewed label gives widely variable daily requirements, not one standard starting schedule. ER interval is at least 6 hours.

fields.contraindication: Mechanical obstruction of the gastrointestinal or urinary tract, and hypersensitivity to anticholinesterase agents.
fields.adverse: Syncope, seizures, severe bradycardia, bronchospasm, and dysrhythmias.
fields.effects: Muscle cramps, increased bronchial secretions, excessive sweating, diarrhea, nausea, and abdominal discomfort.
fields.notes: Dosage must be carefully titrated to the individual patient to balance therapeutic weakness relief against the onset of a cholinergic crisis.

drugs.name: Physostigmine

fields.action: Reversible acetylcholinesterase inhibitor. Unlike other carbamates, it contains a tertiary amine structure, allowing it to readily cross the blood-brain barrier and treat central nervous system effects.
fields.dosage:
FORMS / STRENGTHS
Solution for injection: 1 mg/mL.
DOSE / SCOPE
Selected adult antimuscarinic toxicity: 0.5-2 mg by slow IV administration with cardiac monitoring; toxicology-directed selection and repeat dosing.
fields.indication: Treatment of severe anticholinergic toxicity (e.g., overdose from atropine, scopolamine, or tricyclic antidepressants).
fields.contraindication: Asthma, gangrene, diabetes, cardiovascular disease, mechanical obstruction of the intestinal or urinary tract, and poisoning by depolarizing neuromuscular blockers.
fields.adverse: Seizures, hypersalivation leading to respiratory compromise, bradycardia, asystole, and bronchospasm.
fields.effects: Nausea, vomiting, sweating, dizziness, and restlessness.
fields.notes: Administer via slow IV injection to prevent cardiac arrhythmias and seizures. Atropine should be on hand as a reversing agent if severe cholinergic side effects emerge.

drugs.name: Parathion

fields.action: Irreversible organophosphate acetylcholinesterase inhibitor. It phosphorylates the active site of the enzyme, permanently deactivating it and causing a massive accumulation of acetylcholine across all cholinergic synapses.
fields.dosage:
FORMS / STRENGTHS
Agricultural/industrial formulations (restricted-use pesticide; not an approved clinical pharmaceutical drug).
DOSE / SCOPE
No human therapeutic dose. Agricultural formulations must not be used as medicines.
fields.indication: None clinically (historically used exclusively as an agricultural insecticide/pesticide).
fields.contraindication: N/A (Highly toxic chemical agent; contraindicated for any medical or household use due to extreme mammalian toxicity).
fields.adverse: Fatal respiratory failure, severe pulmonary edema, uncontrollable convulsions, profound bradycardia, complete neuromuscular paralysis, and death.
fields.effects: Profuse sweating, excessive lacrimation, uncontrollable diarrhea, vomiting, muscle fasciculations, miosis, and confusion.
fields.notes: Highly absorbed through skin, lungs, and the GI tract. Treated aggressively with decontamination, high-dose atropine (to block muscarinic signs), and pralidoxime (2-PAM) to regenerate acetylcholinesterase if administered early.

drugs.name: Sarin

fields.action: Extremely potent, irreversible organophosphate nerve agents. They covalently bind to the active serine site of acetylcholinesterase, leading to permanent enzyme inactivation and a toxic, lethal flood of acetylcholine throughout the central and peripheral nervous systems.
fields.dosage:
FORMS / STRENGTHS
Not a pharmaceutical drug; chemical warfare agents.
DOSE / SCOPE
No therapeutic human dose; this is a chemical-hazard entry.
fields.indication: None (classified strictly as weapons of mass destruction / chemical warfare agents).
fields.contraindication: N/A.
fields.adverse: Rapid loss of consciousness, violent convulsions, copious airway secretions, immediate respiratory muscle paralysis, asphyxiation, and death.
fields.effects: Sudden pin-point pupils (miosis), extreme rhinorrhea, intense dyspnea, and uncontrolled body secretions.
fields.notes: Extremely lethal via inhalation or minimal skin contact. Immediate emergency response requires removal from exposure, decontamination, and prompt administration of atropine and pralidoxime alongside an anticonvulsant like diazepam.

drugs.name: Rivastigmine

fields.drug: Rivastigmine. Indirect-acting agents for Alzheimer's disease.
fields.action: Dual inhibitor of both acetylcholinesterase and butyrylcholinesterase (pseudocholinesterase) in the brain, helping to increase cortical levels of acetylcholine.
fields.dosage:
FORMS / STRENGTHS
Oral capsules: 1.5 mg, 3 mg, 4.5 mg, 6 mg. Oral solution: 2 mg/mL. Transdermal patches: 4.6 mg/24hr, 9.5 mg/24hr, 13.3 mg/24hr.
DOSE / SCOPE
Adult oral start: 1.5 mg twice daily with meals. Titrate no faster than every 2 weeks in Alzheimer disease, every 4 weeks in Parkinson dementia; maximum 6 mg twice daily.
fields.indication: Treatment of mild to moderate dementia of the Alzheimer's type and mild to moderate dementia associated with Parkinson's disease.
fields.contraindication: Known hypersensitivity to rivastigmine, other carbamate derivatives, or previous history of application-site contact dermatitis with the rivastigmine patch.
fields.adverse: Severe bradycardia, syncopal episodes, gastrointestinal hemorrhage, and worsening of extrapyramidal symptoms.
fields.effects: Nausea, vomiting, anorexia, weight loss, abdominal pain, dizziness, asthenia, and insomnia.
fields.notes: Oral forms should be taken with food (breakfast and dinner) to reduce gastrointestinal side effects. Patches should be applied daily to clean, dry, hairless skin and rotated to avoid skin irritation.

drugs.name: Galantamine

fields.drug: Galantamine. Indirect-acting agents for Alzheimer's disease.
fields.action: A reversible, competitive acetylcholinesterase inhibitor that also acts as an allosteric modulator at nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, enhancing the action of acetylcholine at nicotinic sites.

Adult immediate release: start 4 mg twice daily with meals; after at least 4 weeks, 8 mg twice daily; further titration to 12 mg twice daily after at least another 4 weeks.

fields.contraindication: Severe renal impairment (creatinine clearance less than 9 mL/min) and severe hepatic impairment.
fields.adverse: Slowed heart rate (bradycardia), heart block, syncope, gastrointestinal bleeding, and increased risk of seizures.
fields.effects: Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, weight loss, decreased appetite, dizziness, headache, and fatigue.
fields.notes: Take with food and ensure adequate fluid intake during treatment to minimize GI side effects. Titrate dosage slowly over intervals of at least 4 weeks.

drugs.name: Atropine

fields.action: Competitive, non-selective muscarinic receptor antagonist that blocks the effects of acetylcholine at parasympathetic neuroeffector sites on smooth muscle, cardiac muscle, and secretory glands.
fields.dosage:
FORMS / STRENGTHS
Injection: 0.1 mg/mL, 0.4 mg/mL, 0.5 mg/mL, 1 mg/mL. Ophthalmic solution: 1%. Eye ointment: 1%.

Adult symptomatic bradycardia (AHA 2025): 1 mg IV, repeat every 3-5 minutes if needed, maximum total 3 mg. Emergency monitoring required.
fields.indication: Preoperative medication to reduce salivary and bronchial secretions, treatment of symptomatic bradycardia, resuscitation during asystole, and as an antidote for organophosphate or nerve agent poisoning.
fields.contraindication: Glaucoma (narrow-angle), obstructive gastrointestinal disease, obstructive uropathy, paralytic ileus, toxic megacolon, and tachycardia secondary to cardiac insufficiency or thyrotoxicosis.
fields.adverse: Ventricular fibrillation, acute psychosis, severe paradoxical bradycardia (with low doses), and anaphylaxis.
fields.effects: Xerostomia (dry mouth), blurred vision, photophobia, tachycardia, constipation, urinary retention, and flushing.
fields.notes: Frequently used as the primary antidote for acute cholinergic toxicity (antidote for organophosphates, carbamates, and muscarinic mushroom poisoning).

fields.action: Reactivates acetylcholinesterase that has been inactivated by organophosphate pesticides or nerve agents. It binds to the organophosphate-enzyme complex, releases the phosphorus atom, and restores normal enzyme activity.

fields.dosage:
FORMS / STRENGTHS
Oral tablets: 12.5 mg, 25 mg, 50 mg. Oral solution: 50 mg/5 mL.

Adult hypertension, reviewed capsule: 12.5 mg once daily; titrate if needed, usually not above 50 mg/day.
fields.indication: Management of essential hypertension and edema associated with congestive heart failure, hepatic cirrhosis, and corticosteroid/estrogen therapy.
fields.contraindication: Anuria, hypersensitivity to sulfonamide-derived drugs, and severe renal or hepatic impairment.

fields.effects: Frequent urination, dizziness, lightheadedness, mild orthostatic hypotension, headache, and fatigue.
fields.notes: Sulfa-allergic patients may cross-react with thiazides; can elevate blood glucose and uric acid levels.

drugs.name: Methyldopa

fields.action: Central alpha-2 adrenergic agonist. It is metabolized intracellularly to alphamethylnorepinephrine, which replaces norepinephrine in vesicles and stimulates central inhibitory alpha-2 receptors, reducing sympathetic vasoconstrictor outflow.
fields.dosage:
FORMS / STRENGTHS
Oral tablets: 250 mg, 500 mg. Intravenous injection: 50 mg/mL.
DOSE / SCOPE
Adult hypertension: start 250 mg 2-3 times daily for 48 hours; then individual titration no more often than every 2 days.

fields.contraindication: Active hepatic disease (such as acute hepatitis or active cirrhosis), previous methyldopa-induced liver disorders, and concurrent use with monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs).
fields.adverse: Drug-induced immune hemolytic anemia (positive direct Coombs test), severe hepatitis, liver necrosis, and parkinsonian signs.
fields.effects: Drowsiness, sedation, dry mouth, nasal stuffiness, edema, dizziness, and postpartum depression.
fields.notes: Widely preferred historically and currently for treating hypertension during pregnancy due to its well-established fetal safety profile, despite routine monitoring required for liver enzymes and Coombs-positive hemolytic anemia.

drugs.name: Dofetilide

fields.action: Selectively blocks the rapid delayed-rectifier potassium current, prolonging repolarization.
fields.dosage:
FORMS / STRENGTHS
Oral capsules: 125, 250, 500 micrograms.
DOSE / SCOPE
Adult AF/flutter initiation: creatinine clearance above 60 mL/min, 500 micrograms twice daily; 40-60, 250 twice daily; 20 to below 40, 125 twice daily. QT-based reduction is required.
fields.indication: Conversion/maintenance of sinus rhythm in selected AF/flutter.
fields.contraindication: Long-QT or excessive baseline QT; creatinine clearance below 20; interacting drugs including verapamil, cimetidine, trimethoprim, ketoconazole and hydrochlorothiazide.
fields.adverse: Torsades and other life-threatening ventricular arrhythmia.
fields.effects: Headache, dizziness, chest discomfort.
fields.notes: Hospital initiation/reinitiation with continuous ECG for at least 3 days. Check the complete interaction list; micrograms are not milligrams.

drugs.name: Adenosine

fields.action: Activates adenosine receptors, briefly slowing or blocking AV-node conduction.
fields.dosage:
FORMS / STRENGTHS
Injection: 3 mg/mL; examples 6 mg/2 mL and 12 mg/4 mL.
DOSE / SCOPE
Adult regular PSVT: 6 mg rapid IV bolus followed immediately by saline flush; if unsuccessful after 1-2 minutes, 12 mg under continuous ECG monitoring.
fields.indication: Rapid conversion of paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia (PSVT) to normal sinus rhythm (including tachycardia associated with accessory bypass tracts like Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome), and diagnostic use during myocardial nuclear imaging.
fields.contraindication: Second- or third-degree AV block, sick sinus syndrome (unless a functioning artificial pacemaker is present), bronchoconstrictive lung disease (such as asthma), and known hypersensitivity to adenosine.
fields.adverse: Transient asystole, severe bronchospasm, heart block, and ventricular arrhythmias.
fields.effects: Flushing (very common), chest pain, shortness of breath, dyspnea, nausea, headache, and lightheadedness.
fields.notes: Possesses an extremely short elimination half-life of less than 10 seconds; must be administered via a rapid intravenous bolus (typically into a peripheral site close to the heart) followed immediately by a saline flush.

drugs.name: Potassium

fields.drug: Potassium. Also listed as Potassium ion; K+. Electrolyte replacement.
fields.action: Restores and maintains normal intracellular potassium concentration, stabilizing the resting membrane potential of cardiac and skeletal muscle cells and regulating neuromuscular excitability.
fields.dosage:
FORMS / STRENGTHS
Example oral potassium chloride ER: 10 or 20 mEq per tablet. State the salt and mEq, not an unspecified mass of potassium.
DOSE / SCOPE
Adult hypokalemia, reviewed oral product: typically 40-100 mEq/day divided; no more than 20 mEq per dose. Adjust to labs and renal function.
fields.indication: Prevention and treatment of hypokalemia (potassium deficiency) due to diuretic use, digitalis toxicity, or excessive losses, and maintenance of cardiac electrophysiological stability.
fields.contraindication: Severe renal impairment (oliguria/anuria), hyperkalemia, acute dehydration, heat cramps, and untreated Addison's disease.
fields.adverse: Hyperkalemia leading to fatal cardiac arrhythmias, ventricular fibrillation, and cardiac arrest.
fields.effects: Nausea, vomiting, abdominal discomfort, diarrhea, and flatulence (especially with oral formulations).
fields.notes: Intravenous potassium must always be heavily diluted and administered via a controlled infusion pump; never give undiluted IV push potassium, as it can cause rapid cardiac arrest.

drugs.name: Magnesium

fields.drug: Magnesium. Also listed as Magnesium ion; Mg2+. Electrolyte replacement / membrane stabilizer.
fields.action: Acts as an essential cofactor for numerous enzymatic reactions and blocks neuromuscular transmission by decreasing acetylcholine release. It regulates sodium, potassium, and calcium movement across cell membranes and controls cardiac excitability.
fields.dosage:
FORMS / STRENGTHS
Intravenous/Intramuscular injection: 50 mg/mL (5%), 125 mg/mL (12.5%), 250 mg/mL (25%), 500 mg/mL (50%). Oral tablets/capsules vary by supplement.
DOSE / SCOPE
Reviewed label, adult mild deficiency: 1 g IM every 6 hours for four doses. This is a product-label example, not a universal regimen. Adjust to labs, kidney function and route; eclampsia and arrhythmia regimens differ.
fields.indication: Treatment and prevention of hypomagnesemia, management of acute torsades de pointes (polymorphic ventricular tachycardia), control of seizures in eclampsia/preeclampsia, and adjunctive treatment of severe acute asthma exacerbations.
fields.contraindication: Myocardial damage, heart block, severe renal insufficiency (risk of hypermagnesemia toxicity), and hypermagnesemia.
fields.adverse: Severe respiratory depression, profound hypotension, complete loss of deep tendon reflexes, and circulatory collapse.
fields.effects: Flushing, sweating, transient hypotension, drowsiness, and local injection-site irritation.
fields.notes: Calcium gluconate must always be kept immediately available as a specific antidote to reverse severe magnesium-induced respiratory depression or toxicity.
